title: SQL vs NoSQL Decision Framework
description: A rigorous decision framework for choosing between SQL and NoSQL databases, backed by real production examples from Netflix, Uber, and Instagram.

segments.text: SQL vs NoSQL is the wrong question. The right question is: what are your access patterns, consistency requirements, and scale constraints? This lesson gives you a decision framework based on real production choices, not marketing hype.

Relational databases excel when your data has relationships and you need flexible queries. PostgreSQL handles complex JOINs across normalized tables, ACID transactions for financial data, and sophisticated indexing. A single Postgres instance can handle 10,000 transactions per second with proper tuning.

Document stores like MongoDB shine when your data is hierarchical and access patterns are known upfront. Key-value stores like DynamoDB deliver single-digit millisecond reads at any scale when you design your partition key correctly. The tradeoff: you give up ad-hoc queries and cross-document transactions.

Start with your access patterns. Are queries known at design time or ad-hoc? If ad-hoc, lean SQL. Do you need multi-record transactions? SQL. Is your data naturally hierarchical with embedded relationships? Document store. Do you need sub-millisecond key lookups at massive scale? Key-value store.

Here's a real scenario. You're building an e-commerce platform. You need product catalog search, shopping cart sessions, order transactions, and recommendation engine storage. Would you use one database or multiple? Which types?
segments.thought_prompt: For each e-commerce domain (catalog, cart, orders, recommendations), which database type would you choose and why?

segments.text: Netflix uses polyglot persistence. Cassandra for high-throughput writes like viewing history. EVCache, built on Memcached, for session data. MySQL for billing transactions. Elasticsearch for search. Each database handles what it's best at. The cost: operational complexity and data synchronization challenges.

Uber famously migrated from PostgreSQL to MySQL plus Schemaless, their custom NoSQL layer. The issue wasn't SQL itself — it was write amplification from Postgres's MVCC implementation causing replication lag. Their write-heavy workload amplified WAL size by 10 to 20x. They kept Postgres for other services where it fit.

DynamoDB guarantees single-digit millisecond performance at any scale, but only if your partition key distributes evenly. A common mistake: using a date as partition key. All writes for today hit one partition, causing hot partition throttling. Instagram solved this by prefixing user_id to distribute writes.

MongoDB makes sense when your data is truly document-shaped. Content management systems, product catalogs with varying attributes, user profiles with nested preferences. It struggles when you need cross-collection joins. MongoDB added transactions in 4.0, but multi-document transactions add latency and complexity.

NewSQL databases like CockroachDB and TiDB promise SQL semantics with NoSQL scalability. CockroachDB uses Raft consensus and automatic sharding while supporting full SQL. The tradeoff: higher write latency due to consensus rounds, typically 10 to 50 milliseconds. For read-heavy workloads, they're compelling.

The CAP theorem isn't a choice between three options — it's a spectrum. Postgres gives you CP with strong consistency. DynamoDB can be configured for AP with eventual consistency or CP with strong reads. The real question is: which consistency model can your business logic tolerate?
segments.thought_prompt: For a payment system, can you ever accept eventual consistency? What about a social media likes counter?

segments.text: Stop choosing databases based on hype. Start with your access patterns, consistency needs, and operational capacity. Most production systems end up polyglot. The key is picking the right tool for each domain and having a clear strategy for keeping data synchronized across stores.
